title: ICC Associate Translation Coordination Officer (P-2) in The Hague, Netherlands: International Criminal Court Job Opportunity 2026
summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is inviting applications for the position of Associate Translation Coordination Officer (P-2) within its Language Services Unit , based in The Hague, Netherlands . This is an established professional position within the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) and offers an opportunity for qualified language, translation, linguistics, and related professionals to contribute to the work of an international judicial institution responsible for investigating and prosecuting serious international crimes. The position is particularly relevant to professionals with experience in translation, language services, linguistics, transcription, computer-assisted translation (CAT), machine translation (MT), and coordination of multilingual language operations . The selected candidate will support the Translation Officer in coordinating high-quality translation and transcription services required by the Office of the Prosecutor, with a particular emphasis on situation languages . The application deadline is 13 September 2026 at midnight, The Hague time . International Criminal Court Associate Translation Coordination Officer Job 2026 The vacancy is identified as: Job title: Associate Translation Coordination Officer Grade: P-2 Requisition ID: 24501 Post number: E-1104 Organizational unit: Language Services Unit, Integrated Services Division, Office of the Prosecutor Duty station: The Hague, Netherlands Appointment type: Established Post Contract: Initial two-year appointment, with possibility of extension Probation: Six months Minimum net annual salary: €71,403 Application deadline: 13 September 2026, midnight The Hague time The selection process may also result in the establishment of a roster of suitable candidates for future fixed-term appointments against established posts and positions funded through general temporary assistance. This means that the recruitment exercise may potentially serve not only the immediate vacancy but also future staffing requirements within the relevant area. About the International Criminal Court The International Criminal Court is an international judicial institution dealing with individuals accused of some of the most serious crimes of concern to the international community. The work of the Court depends on highly specialized professionals across legal, investigative, analytical, technological, administrative, linguistic, and operational functions. Language services are particularly important because the Court s work involves evidence, testimony, documents, audio and video materials, investigations, prosecutions, and communication across multiple languages. For the Office of the Prosecutor, accurate and timely translation and transcription can be essential to ensuring that evidence and information can be assessed and used effectively. The Associate Translation Coordination Officer will therefore work in an environment where accuracy, confidentiality, organization, multilingual communication, and strict deadlines are critical. About the Office of the Prosecutor and Integrated Services Division The position is located within the Integrated Services Division (ISD) of the Office of the Prosecutor. The Integrated Services Division brings together specialized support functions that provide cross-cutting assistance to the Office of the Prosecutor. The Division is responsible for ensuring that the Office has reliable and cost-effective access to the services, technologies, expertise, and equipment required to carry out its mandate. Its areas of support include: Information, knowledge, and evidence management Forensic science Language services Tracking Information fusion Technology and modern tools Other specialized operational support functions The Division also works to develop new approaches and strategies that can improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the Office of the Prosecutor. About the Language Services Unit The Language Services Unit (LSU) forms part of the Integrated Services Division and provides specialized language support to the Office of the Prosecutor. Its work supports different phases of the Office s activities, including: Preliminary examinations Investigations Prosecution The Unit provides a wide range of language-related services, including: Field interpretation Event interpretation Remote interpretation Audio transcription Video transcription Translation of evidence Translation of core Office documentation Summary translation Redacting Editing Other specialized language services Because these services can directly support investigations and prosecutions, the Unit must maintain high standards of accuracy, confidentiality, consistency, and timeliness. What Will the Associate Translation Coordination Officer Do? The successful candidate will work within the Language Services Unit and report to the Translation Officer . The central responsibility will be to support the coordination and delivery of high-quality translation and transcription services for the Office of the Prosecutor. The role will involve both operational coordination and technical language-service responsibilities. 1. Coordinate Translation and Transcription Services The Associate Translation Coordination Officer will support the Translation Officer in ensuring that translation and transcription requests are delivered: On time At an appropriate level of quality In a form suitable for the intended purpose In accordance with operational requirements The role will focus mainly on situation languages . The officer will need to proactively plan language-service assignments and determine how different requests can be handled effectively. Responsibilities will include: Planning translation workloads Prioritizing requests Assessing feasibility Coordinating assignments Assigning work to staff translators Assigning work to staff transcribers Coordinating external freelance translators Monitoring delivery Supporting quality and consistency This makes the position particularly suitable for someone who combines strong language expertise with excellent organizational and coordination skills. 2. Identify and Evaluate Translators The officer will also contribute to identifying suitable language professionals who can meet the Court s translation requirements. This may include: Identifying freelance translators Testing translators Evaluating translator performance Selecting suitable freelance professionals Supporting the identification of translation staff Matching language expertise to operational requirements The focus will particularly be on situation languages , meaning languages relevant to the situations and investigations being handled by the Office of the Prosecutor. This responsibility requires the ability to assess not only language proficiency but also translation quality, reliability, professional standards, and suitability for specialized work. 3. Support Translator Induction and Training The Associate Translation Coordination Officer will support the Translation Officer in the induction and training of new translators. This will primarily involve translators working with situation languages. The role may therefore involve helping new translators understand: Translation requirements Institutional procedures Quality standards Workflows Confidentiality expectations Relevant tools Documentation standards Specialized terminology Operational requirements The position therefore includes an element of coaching and capacity development . 4. Support Quality Assurance Quality assurance is another important part of the role. The successful candidate will assist in developing and implementing mechanisms designed to ensure that translation work remains: Accurate Consistent Reliable Fit for purpose Aligned with institutional standards This may involve contributing to quality-control processes and identifying opportunities to improve translation workflows. Candidates should therefore be comfortable dealing with complex linguistic issues and identifying potential translation problems. 5. Develop Translation Guidelines and Procedures The Associate Translation Coordination Officer will contribute to the development, updating, and implementation of: Translation guidelines Procedures Workflows Operational practices Particular attention will be given to processes related to situation languages . This responsibility means that the position is not limited to completing individual translation-related tasks. The officer will also contribute to improving the systems through which language services are delivered. 6. Monitor Workloads and Support Planning The officer will support the Translation Officer in monitoring workload levels across language-service activities. This includes contributing to: Workload monitoring Human resources planning Budget planning Staffing recommendations Resource allocation The position therefore requires an understanding of how language-service operations can be managed efficiently in a high-pressure international environment. 7. Perform Other Related Duties As with many international professional positions, the successful candidate may also be required to undertake other related responsibilities assigned within the scope of the position. Flexibility will therefore be important. Educational Requirements Applicants must have an advanced university degree in one of the following or a relevant related field: Languages Linguistics Translation Another relevant field However, the vacancy provides an alternative route. A first-level university degree may be accepted in place of an advanced degree if it is combined with two additional years of qualifying professional experience . This means candidates should carefully assess both their academic qualifications and relevant professional experience before applying. Professional Experience Requirements The position requires a minimum of two years of relevant professional experience . Relevant areas include: Translation Linguistics Language-service provision Other relevant professional fields For candidates applying with a first-level university degree instead of an advanced degree, the requirement increases to four years of qualifying professional experience . The experience should be relevant to the responsibilities of the position rather than simply general employment experience. Required Experience With CAT and MT Tools Experience using computer-assisted translation (CAT) and machine translation (MT) tools is specifically required. This is an important requirement for applicants because the position involves modern translation workflows and language-service technologies. Knowledge of relevant software, including CAT tools such as memoQ , is particularly relevant. Candidates should therefore highlight practical experience with: CAT tools MT tools Translation-management workflows Digital document systems Office productivity software where applicable. International Organization Experience Experience working within an international organization is described as highly desirable. While it is not listed as an essential requirement, candidates with experience in international organizations may have an advantage because they may already understand: Multicultural working environments Institutional procedures International professional standards Confidentiality requirements Multilingual operations Complex organizational workflows Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities The ICC is looking for a combination of technical language expertise, operational coordination skills, interpersonal capabilities, and professional judgment. Organizational and Planning Skills Applicants should demonstrate excellent: Organizational skills Analytical skills Planning skills Prioritization abilities Time-management skills The position requires managing multiple language-service requests while balancing deadlines, resources, quality, and operational priorities. Leadership and Coaching The successful candidate should have: Leadership skills Managerial skills Coaching abilities Capacity to support other translators These capabilities will be particularly relevant to translator induction, training, task coordination, and quality assurance. Linguistic and Analytical Expertise Applicants should be able to understand complex: Linguistic issues Translation challenges Terminology matters Language-service requirements This is especially important given the role s focus on specialized translation and situation languages. Technology Skills Candidates should have sound knowledge of relevant computer software, particularly: CAT tools MT tools Office suites Electronic document management systems Experience with tools such as memoQ is specifically highlighted. Communication Skills The role requires strong: Interpersonal skills Listening skills Written communication Oral communication The successful candidate will communicate with translators, transcribers, staff members, managers, and potentially external language professionals. Negotiation and Problem-Solving Applicants should demonstrate: Negotiation skills Problem-solving abilities Decision-making skills These are particularly important when managing competing priorities, translation assignments, deadlines, resources, and quality requirements. Ability to Work Under Pressure The position involves evolving priorities and potentially tight deadlines. Candidates should therefore be able to work: Flexibly Effectively under pressure Within strict deadlines With changing priorities Language Requirements Language proficiency is a central component of this position. The candidate must have proficiency in at least one of the ICC s working languages: English or French . Working knowledge of the other working language is desirable. Additional language skills can strengthen a candidate s profile. Knowledge of another official language of the Court is an asset. These include: Arabic Chinese Russian Spanish Knowledge of a situation-related language is also considered an asset. Examples listed in the vacancy include: Ukrainian Burmese Dari Pashto Tagalog Cebuano Hebrew Swahili Applicants with relevant language combinations should make these capabilities clear in their application. ICC Leadership Competencies The vacancy identifies four leadership competencies that are relevant to the position: Purpose Collaboration People Results These competencies reflect the importance of connecting the Court s mission with effective teamwork, people management, and achievement of operational results. Salary and Contract The position offers a minimum net annual salary of €71,403 . The appointment is an established post . For initial appointments, the Court offers: A two-year appointment Possibility of extension Six-month probationary period The position is based in The Hague, Netherlands . Nationality and Eligibility Requirements One of the most important eligibility conditions concerns nationality. The vacancy states that the post is to be filled by a national of a State Party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court , or by a national of a state that: Has signed the Rome Statute and is engaged in the ratification process; or Is engaged in the accession process. This requirement is linked to an ICC Assembly of States Parties decision introducing a moratorium on recruitment of staff who are nationals of states that are not States Parties to the Rome Statute. Therefore, nationality is a significant eligibility consideration for this position. Applicants should verify their country s current status under the Rome Statute before submitting an application. Gender and Geographical Representation The ICC states that it aims to achieve fair representation of women and men across its positions. It also seeks equitable geographical representation within the Professional category. The vacancy specifically states that applications from female candidates are particularly encouraged . There is no race-based eligibility restriction stated in the vacancy. The relevant eligibility distinction is primarily based on nationality and the applicant s country s relationship to the Rome Statute . Personnel Security Clearance The successful candidate will be subject to a Personnel Security Clearance (PSC) process. According to the vacancy, this process will include, among other checks: Verification of information provided in the personal history form Criminal record check Candidates should therefore ensure that all information submitted during the application and recruitment process is accurate and complete. Click HERE to read more. Application Deadline The deadline for applications is: 13 September 2026 at midnight, The Hague time. Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their application, particularly because international professional vacancies can require applicants to gather detailed education, employment, language, and professional information. APPLY HERE Conclusion The International Criminal Court Associate Translation Coordination Officer (P-2) vacancy offers a professional opportunity for experienced language and translation specialists to contribute to the work of the Court from its headquarters in The Hague, Netherlands . Proficiency in English or French is required, while knowledge of the other working language, additional official ICC languages, or situation-related languages can strengthen an applicant s profile. The position offers a minimum net annual salary of €71,403 , an initial two-year appointment with the possibility of extension, and a six-month probationary period. Most importantly, applicants should carefully check the nationality requirement , as the vacancy is restricted to nationals of eligible ICC States Parties or nationals of states that fall within the specified ratification or accession categories. The application deadline is 13 September 2026 at midnight, The Hague time . Click HERE for more job opportunities. title: UNITAR Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction Training Programme 2026: Apply for Free UN Training on Disaster Preparedness and Inclusive Leadership
summary: The United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) has opened applications for the Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction Training Programme for World Tsunami Awareness Day 2026 , a Japan-funded learning opportunity designed to strengthen disaster risk reduction knowledge, leadership capacity and community resilience across the Asia-Pacific region. The programme is seeking 500 motivated participants of all genders aged 18 and above , with particular relevance to people living in or originating from Pacific Island countries and territories and Asian countries. Participants will receive free training in disaster risk reduction, inclusive leadership, climate-related risks, community resilience, communication and disaster preparedness. According to UNITAR, the programme will draw on both the Asia-Pacific context and Japan’s experience with natural hazards to help participants develop practical disaster risk reduction plans that respond to the specific needs of their communities and countries. The official UNITAR announcement confirms that the programme is offered free of charge with financial support from the Government and People of Japan. Opportunity Overview Programme: UNITAR Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction Training Programme for World Tsunami Awareness Day 2026 Theme: Building Economies and Livelihoods Resilient to Global Shocks Organiser: United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Funding: Government and People of Japan Number of participants: Approximately 500 Gender: All genders are welcome Age requirement: 18 years and above Language: English Format: Online learning, followed by specialized training for top-performing participants Programme period: August 2026 to March 2027 Cost: Free Certificate: UNITAR certificate for participants who complete all requirements Application deadline: 21 August 2026 at 11:59 p.m. JST (UTC+9) UNITAR s official announcement confirms the 21 August 2026 deadline and the target of 500 participants. What Is the UNITAR Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction Programme? The UNITAR Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction Training Programme is designed to help individuals develop the knowledge, leadership capabilities and practical skills required to contribute to disaster preparedness, prevention, response and resilience. Although the programme places a strong emphasis on women s leadership, it is not restricted exclusively to women . UNITAR explicitly states that motivated learners of all genders are welcome. The programme also welcomes applicants from outside the priority geographical areas, while noting that the learning content is particularly contextualized to the Pacific Islands and Asia. The initiative reflects UNITAR s broader work on leadership, empowerment and inclusive disaster risk reduction. UNITAR identifies inclusive leadership, women s leadership, effective communication, project development and inclusive disaster risk reduction planning among its focus areas. The programme is particularly relevant at a time when communities are facing increasingly complex risks associated with natural hazards, climate change, environmental degradation, economic disruptions and other global shocks. Rather than focusing exclusively on theoretical knowledge, the training is structured to help participants translate what they learn into practical disaster risk reduction planning for their own communities and countries. Why This Programme Matters Disasters can have disproportionate effects on vulnerable communities, particularly where people have limited access to resources, infrastructure, information and decision-making opportunities. Effective disaster risk reduction therefore requires more than emergency response. Communities need leaders who understand risk, can communicate effectively, can identify vulnerable groups, can work across sectors and can develop plans that incorporate local knowledge and community priorities. The UNITAR programme addresses these needs by combining: Disaster risk reduction education Leadership development Gender-inclusive approaches Community-based planning Climate change considerations Ecosystem-based approaches Nature-based solutions Indigenous and traditional knowledge Communication and media skills Understanding of vulnerable groups Practical disaster risk reduction planning Lessons from Japanese disaster experiences UNITAR s wider disaster risk reduction work emphasizes empowering women and other vulnerable groups with inclusive leadership skills that can strengthen communities and institutions. Programme Structure The 2026 programme is divided into two major phases . Phase I: Online Learning Period: August to November 2026 Approximately 500 selected participants will take part in the first phase through online learning. The online phase is designed to establish a strong foundation in disaster risk reduction and inclusive leadership. Participants will be expected to: Complete self-paced online learning modules. Participate in webinars featuring experts. Complete assignments. Study disaster risk reduction concepts. Examine international frameworks and development goals. Explore community and ecosystem-based approaches. Develop an individual disaster risk reduction plan. Reflect on leadership, gender and resilience. Apply lessons to their own communities and countries. The online format makes the first phase accessible to participants across different countries and territories without requiring international travel. Phase II: Specialized Training With Experts The strongest performers from Phase I will be invited to participate in specialized training with experts. For participants from Asia and non-Pacific countries , the specialized workshop is scheduled to take place online in February 2027 . For participants from Pacific countries , the specialized workshop is scheduled to take place in person in March 2027 . The second phase will provide opportunities to engage with regional and international institutions, academics and humanitarian experts through specialized lectures, discussions and other learning activities. For Pacific participants, the in-person component is expected to include study tours in addition to lectures and discussions. Important Note About the Phase II Dates The information provided for the 2026 programme indicates that the Pacific Phase II workshop will take place in March 2027 . This is consistent with the programme s two-phase timeline beginning in 2026. Applicants should therefore distinguish the 2027 Phase II workshop from previous cycles of the programme. UNITAR s 2025 cycle, for example, had its specialized training in March 2026. Learning Objectives One of the strongest aspects of the UNITAR training is its practical learning approach. By completing Phase I, participants are expected to develop a foundational understanding of disaster risk reduction and apply that knowledge to planning. Phase I Learning Objectives Participants will learn to: Develop basic knowledge and understanding of disaster risk reduction concepts. Discuss fundamental principles of disaster risk reduction. Understand the relevance of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. Connect disaster risk reduction with the Sustainable Development Goals. Understand ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction. Explain community-based disaster risk reduction approaches. Develop an inclusive country-level disaster risk reduction plan. Examine lessons from Japan s experience with natural hazards. Study lessons from the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami. Examine lessons from the 2018 West Japan Floods. Understand the importance of gender-inclusive leadership. Examine women s leadership in disaster risk reduction. Explore norms, challenges and best practices relating to women s leadership in the Pacific and Japan. These objectives are designed to help participants move beyond simply understanding disasters to considering how communities can systematically identify, reduce and manage risks. Phase II Learning Objectives Participants selected for the second phase will develop more advanced skills. These include: Understanding the characteristics required for effective leadership and management. Developing a technical understanding of hazards. Learning about hazard assessment tools. Improving communication skills relevant to disaster risk reduction. Developing communication skills for working with the media. Understanding the specific needs of vulnerable groups. Exploring nature-based solutions. Appreciating Indigenous and traditional knowledge. Understanding local approaches to resilience. Examining additional risks associated with disasters. Understanding stress and mental health risks in disaster contexts. The second phase therefore moves toward more specialized leadership and practical application. Practical Assignments The programme is not simply based on watching lectures or completing passive online lessons. Participants will have practical assignments designed to demonstrate their ability to apply the concepts they learn. Phase I Assignment Participants will be required to: Prepare and submit an individual disaster risk reduction plan. This assignment provides an opportunity to apply the training to a real community or national context. A strong plan could demonstrate an applicant s understanding of: Major hazards affecting their community. Vulnerable groups. Existing preparedness measures. Potential gaps in disaster planning. Community resources. Local knowledge. Environmental considerations. Inclusive leadership. Communication strategies. Potential prevention and mitigation measures. Recovery and resilience considerations. Phase II Assignment Participants progressing to Phase II will be expected to: Prepare and present an individual project. This provides an additional opportunity for selected participants to demonstrate leadership, analytical thinking, communication and practical problem-solving skills. Key Benefits of Participating Although applicants should not approach the programme solely for the certificate, there are several valuable outcomes associated with participating. 1. Free International Training The programme is offered free of charge , with financial support from the Government and People of Japan. This removes the tuition barrier that can prevent many professionals, young leaders and community practitioners from accessing international training. 2. Disaster Risk Reduction Skills Participants will gain knowledge relevant to: Disaster preparedness Risk assessment Community resilience Disaster planning Climate-related risks Emergency preparedness Vulnerability assessment Nature-based solutions Community-based disaster risk reduction 3. Leadership Development The programme specifically emphasizes leadership and management. Participants can strengthen their ability to: Lead teams. Communicate during risk situations. Engage communities. Work with different stakeholders. Develop inclusive plans. Advocate for disaster preparedness. Support vulnerable populations. 4. Exposure to Japanese Disaster Risk Reduction Experience Japan has extensive experience dealing with earthquakes, tsunamis, floods and other natural hazards. The programme gives participants an opportunity to study lessons from Japanese experiences, including the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami and the 2018 West Japan Floods . 5. Understanding Gender-Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction A key focus of the programme is recognizing the role that gender and inclusive leadership play in disaster preparedness and response. Participants will explore the importance of ensuring that disaster planning reflects the needs and experiences of different groups within society. 6. Practical Planning Experience Participants will develop an individual disaster risk reduction plan during Phase I. This can help them develop practical experience that may be useful in community development, humanitarian work, climate action, disaster management, public policy and related fields. 7. Expert Engagement Selected Phase II participants will have opportunities to learn from experts and engage with regional and international institutions, academics and humanitarian professionals. 8. UNITAR Certificate Participants who complete all programme requirements will receive a UNITAR certificate . This can provide formal recognition of participation and completion of the training. Who Should Apply? The programme is particularly suitable for individuals who have a genuine interest in disaster risk reduction, climate change, community resilience and leadership. Potential applicants may include: Community leaders Youth leaders Women leaders Climate change advocates Disaster risk reduction practitioners Humanitarian workers Development professionals Civil society representatives Community development practitioners Emergency preparedness professionals Environmental advocates Public-sector professionals Educators and trainers Researchers Students and graduates with relevant interests Individuals working on community resilience Professionals interested in inclusive leadership A formal university degree is not identified as a mandatory eligibility requirement in the stated criteria. Instead, UNITAR emphasizes age, motivation, English proficiency, computer literacy, internet access, interest in disaster risk reduction and commitment to completing the programme. Eligibility Requirements Applicants should meet the following requirements: Age Applicants must be 18 years old or above . Interest in Leadership and Disaster Risk Reduction Applicants should be eager to learn about the leadership skills required for disaster risk reduction. Passion for Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Applicants should demonstrate an interest in climate change, disaster risk reduction and the effects of disasters on communities. Community Impact Applicants should be motivated to succeed and make a positive contribution to their communities. English Proficiency The programme is conducted in English , so applicants should have sufficient English-language ability to participate in learning activities, webinars, assignments and discussions. Computer Literacy Applicants must be comfortable using computers and participating in online learning. Internet Access Because Phase I is delivered online, applicants need reliable access to the internet. Commitment Applicants must be prepared to complete the programme requirements, including online modules, webinars and assignments. Countries and Regions Encouraged to Apply UNITAR particularly encourages applications from Pacific Island countries and territories and countries in Asia. Pacific Island Countries Applicants from the following Pacific countries are specifically encouraged to participate: Cook Islands Federated States of Micronesia Fiji Kiribati Marshall Islands Nauru Niue Palau Papua New Guinea Samoa Solomon Islands Tonga Tuvalu Vanuatu Asian Countries Applicants from the following Asian countries are specifically encouraged to apply: Bangladesh Brunei Cambodia India Indonesia Iran Malaysia Maldives Myanmar Pakistan Philippines Sri Lanka Thailand Timor-Leste Viet Nam UNITAR s broader leadership and disaster risk reduction portfolio also identifies Asia and Pacific Island countries as important geographical focus areas. Can Applicants From Other Countries Apply? Yes. One important aspect of this opportunity is that the programme is not strictly limited to nationals of the listed countries . UNITAR states that learners from other parts of the world are also welcome to participate, provided they understand that the training materials are contextualized toward the Pacific Islands and Asia. Therefore, applicants from outside the priority countries should not automatically assume they are ineligible. However, applicants from the Pacific Islands and Asia are the principal geographical groups highlighted in the call. Is This Programme Fully Online? The programme begins with an online learning phase. From August to November 2026, participants will complete online modules, participate in webinars and undertake assignments. The second phase depends on geography: Asia and non-Pacific participants: Online specialized workshop in February 2027. Pacific participants: In-person specialized workshop in March 2027. Applicants should therefore be prepared for online participation regardless of their location and understand that successful Pacific participants may later be invited to an in-person component. Is the Programme Fully Funded? The training itself is offered free of charge because it is financially supported by the Government and People of Japan. However, applicants should carefully review the official application information for any logistical arrangements associated with Phase II, particularly for participants selected for in-person activities. The fact that the training is free should not automatically be interpreted as a guarantee that every personal expense associated with participation will be covered unless UNITAR explicitly states so. Why Women’s Leadership Is Central to the Programme The programme s emphasis on women s leadership reflects the recognition that women play an important role in disaster preparedness, community resilience and recovery. At the same time, UNITAR s approach is inclusive of other genders. This combination is important because disaster risk reduction requires an all-of-society approach. Communities need decision-making processes that consider the different risks, responsibilities, capacities and experiences of the people affected by disasters. UNITAR describes its women s leadership and disaster risk reduction work as supporting vulnerable groups, inclusive leadership and community empowerment. Connection With the Sendai Framework and Sustainable Development Goals The programme introduces participants to major international approaches to disaster risk reduction. One of these is the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction , which provides an international framework for reducing disaster risk and strengthening resilience. Participants will also examine the relationship between disaster risk reduction and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) . This is important because disasters can undermine development progress by damaging infrastructure, disrupting livelihoods, increasing poverty and inequality, affecting health and education and placing additional pressure on communities and governments. Integrating disaster risk reduction into development planning can therefore help communities build resilience while pursuing broader development objectives. Ecosystem-Based and Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction The programme also goes beyond conventional disaster management. Participants will explore ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction , which recognizes the role that healthy ecosystems can play in reducing disaster risks. They will also examine community-based disaster risk reduction , emphasizing the importance of involving communities directly in understanding risks and designing solutions. This approach recognizes that communities often possess valuable local knowledge about hazards, vulnerabilities, traditional coping mechanisms and resilience strategies. Indigenous and Traditional Knowledge Phase II includes a deeper exploration of Indigenous and traditional knowledge. This is particularly relevant to Pacific communities and other locations where traditional knowledge plays an important role in environmental management, disaster preparedness and community resilience. Combining scientific knowledge with local and traditional knowledge can help produce disaster risk reduction strategies that are more relevant to the people and environments they are intended to serve. Communication and Media Skills Disaster risk reduction is not only about technical planning. Effective communication is essential before, during and after disasters. Participants in the advanced phase will explore communication for disaster risk reduction and the media. These skills can be valuable for professionals who may need to: Communicate risks to the public. Explain preparedness measures. Share emergency information. Work with journalists. Counter misinformation. Communicate with vulnerable groups. Coordinate with stakeholders. Promote community preparedness. Understanding Vulnerable Groups The programme also emphasizes understanding the needs of vulnerable groups. This is an important component of inclusive disaster risk reduction because the effects of disasters are not experienced equally. Effective planning should consider the needs of different populations and ensure that disaster preparedness strategies do not exclude people who may face additional barriers during emergencies. Stress and Mental Health Risks Disasters can produce significant psychological and social pressures. Phase II participants will therefore also explore other risks, including stress and mental health risks . This broadens the concept of resilience beyond physical infrastructure and emergency response to include the human and social dimensions of disaster recovery. About UNITAR The United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) is the dedicated training arm of the United Nations. Established in 1965, UNITAR works to strengthen knowledge and skills through training, research and innovative learning solutions. Its work is delivered through partnerships and a global learning platform, with a particular focus on strengthening individuals, institutions and organizations and supporting progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals and other international priorities. UNITAR s work includes programmes focused on leadership, disaster risk reduction, sustainable development, climate action, peace and security, and other areas of international development. Its leadership and empowerment portfolio specifically includes women s leadership, effective communication, project development, gender mainstreaming and inclusive disaster risk reduction planning. How to Apply Interested applicants should apply through the official UNITAR application process rather than submitting an application by email. Applicants should: Review the official programme information carefully. Confirm that they meet the age, language, technology and commitment requirements. Prepare the information required for the application. Submit the application through the official online application platform. Complete the application before the stated deadline. Keep a record of the submitted application and any confirmation received. UNITAR specifically states that applications will not be accepted by email . For programme enquiries, UNITAR lists the Hiroshima Project Office contact email as DRR-Prosperity@unitar.org , but applicants should use the designated online application process rather than sending their application to that address. Official programme information: UNITAR – Women’s Leadership in Disaster Risk Reduction for World Tsunami Awareness Day 2026 Application Deadline The deadline for applications is: 21 August 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Japan Standard Time (JST), UTC+9. Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their applications. Differences between local time zones, internet connectivity problems and incomplete application information can create unnecessary last-minute challenges. Applicants outside Japan should convert the deadline to their local time and submit well before the closing time. Pro Tip for Applicants Applicants should avoid treating this as a generic online course application. A strong application should clearly communicate a genuine interest in disaster risk reduction, climate resilience, leadership and community impact . Where the application provides opportunities to explain motivation or experience, applicants should consider highlighting: Their involvement in community initiatives. Experience working with vulnerable communities. Interest in climate change or environmental issues. Disaster preparedness or humanitarian experience. Leadership responsibilities. Volunteer activities. Communication or advocacy experience. Examples of how they have contributed to positive community change. Their understanding of the disaster risks affecting their community. How they intend to apply the knowledge gained through UNITAR. Most importantly, applicants should demonstrate that they intend to use the training beyond the classroom . The programme instead emphasizes age, motivation, English proficiency, computer literacy, internet access and commitment. Do I need professional disaster management experience? Not according to the stated eligibility requirements. Applicants need to demonstrate an interest in disaster risk reduction and leadership and a desire to make a positive impact. Is English required? Yes. The programme will be delivered in English, and applicants are expected to be proficient in English. Can applicants outside Asia and the Pacific apply? Yes. UNITAR states that applicants from other parts of the world are welcome, although the content is contextualized toward the Pacific Islands and Asia. With approximately 500 participants expected, the programme offers a structured pathway from foundational online learning to more specialized training for top-performing participants. Its focus on inclusive leadership, community-based disaster risk reduction, gender-responsive approaches, climate change, nature-based solutions, Indigenous knowledge, communication and resilience makes it particularly relevant to people working or aspiring to work in humanitarian action, development, climate change, disaster management and community leadership. Applicants from Pacific Island countries and territories and Asia are particularly encouraged to apply, while people from other regions are also welcome. title: VALUE4HER Climate Adaptation Evidence and Finance Readiness Facility for Women-Led Agribusiness SMEs
summary: Women-led agribusinesses across Africa are playing an increasingly important role in strengthening food-system resilience and responding to the growing impacts of climate change. From climate-smart production and aggregation to processing, input distribution, logistics, advisory services, and market access, women entrepreneurs are developing practical solutions that help businesses and communities adapt to climate risks. However, many of these efforts remain poorly documented. The adaptation practices being implemented by small and medium-sized agribusinesses are often not captured in formal climate adaptation evidence systems, investment materials, policy discussions, or climate finance reporting. The VALUE4HER Climate Adaptation Evidence and Finance Readiness Facility for Women-Led Agribusiness SMEs seeks to address this gap by helping selected women-led agribusiness SMEs identify, organize, strengthen, package, and communicate the climate adaptation evidence they already generate through their businesses. The initiative is anchored in VALUE4HER , AGRA’s flagship platform for women-led agribusinesses, and implemented through a partnership between AGRA and CGIAR , specifically the Alliance of Bioversity International-CIAT and the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). The initiative combines VALUE4HER’s extensive network and SME engagement infrastructure with CGIAR’s technical expertise in climate adaptation tracking, impact measurement, risk intelligence, climate finance readiness, evidence synthesis, and gender-responsive adaptation. What Is the VALUE4HER Climate Adaptation Evidence and Finance Readiness Facility? The facility is designed as a practical support mechanism for women-led agribusiness SMEs that are already taking action to address climate risks but need support to demonstrate the value and impact of those actions. Rather than primarily financing new research or requiring SMEs to undertake extensive primary data collection, the initiative focuses on helping businesses make better use of information and evidence that already exists within their operations. This may include: Production records Business performance data Market information Climate-risk information Adoption data Customer or farmer data Extension and advisory records Operational information Resilience-related business outcomes Existing monitoring and evaluation data Information on climate adaptation practices Evidence of changes in productivity, market access, efficiency, or business continuity The facility will help participating SMEs transform such information into credible and useful evidence products that can support: Climate adaptation learning Business growth Investor engagement Climate finance readiness Policy engagement Adaptation reporting Evidence-based decision-making Visibility of women s contributions to climate action Implementing Partners The initiative will be implemented through collaboration between AGRA and CGIAR , drawing on the complementary strengths of the participating organizations. AGRA and VALUE4HER VALUE4HER is AGRA’s flagship platform supporting women-led agribusinesses across Africa. The platform provides access to and facilitates opportunities related to: Finance Markets Technology Mentoring Networking Capacity building Business development VALUE4HER reaches more than 17,000 women-led agribusinesses across 46 African countries , providing a significant platform through which promising SMEs can be identified, targeted, supported, and connected. For this initiative, VALUE4HER will serve as an important: Delivery platform Targeting mechanism SME engagement channel Learning platform Selection and onboarding pathway AGRA will also contribute its climate adaptation technical capacity to help identify women-led SMEs that are already contributing to climate adaptation. CGIAR CGIAR will contribute technical expertise through the Adaptation Insights project , with relevant expertise from the Alliance of Bioversity International-CIAT and ILRI. CGIAR’s contribution will include technical support related to: Climate adaptation tracking Impact measurement Climate-risk intelligence Climate finance readiness Evidence packaging Technical masterclasses Evidence synthesis Gender-responsive adaptation Learning and knowledge generation The partnership therefore brings together a strong SME network with specialized climate adaptation and evidence capabilities. Overall Goal of the Initiative The overall goal is to leverage VALUE4HER as a platform for strengthening the capacity of women-led agribusiness SMEs to document, package, and communicate climate adaptation evidence in ways that improve climate finance readiness, enhance resilience, and increase the visibility of women’s contributions to climate action and adaptation reporting. The initiative therefore connects three important areas: Climate adaptation + credible evidence + finance readiness The ultimate ambition is to make women s climate adaptation contributions more visible, more credible, and more useful for investment, policy, learning, and future scaling. Specific Objectives The facility has five major objectives. 1. Identify women-led agribusiness SMEs with adaptation potential Through VALUE4HER, the initiative will identify women-led agribusiness SMEs that have: Existing climate adaptation practices Exposure to climate risks Relevant operational evidence Potential for business growth Interest in climate finance Potential to generate useful adaptation evidence 2. Strengthen evidence management capacity Selected SMEs will receive support to organize, validate, package, and communicate the climate adaptation information they already have. The focus is on making existing business evidence more structured, credible, understandable, and useful. 3. Improve climate finance and investment readiness The initiative will help SMEs translate their adaptation experience and evidence into business-relevant narratives and materials. This can help businesses better communicate with: Investors Financial institutions Climate finance providers Development finance actors Corporate partners Other potential funders 4. Generate a synthesized evidence base The initiative will synthesize information from participating businesses to develop a broader understanding of: Women s climate adaptation practices Business benefits of adaptation Resilience outcomes Climate-related business risks Evidence gaps Finance-readiness needs Opportunities for scaling 5. Support gender-responsive adaptation reporting and policy engagement By making women s adaptation activities more visible, the initiative can contribute to broader climate adaptation measurement, policy discussions, learning, and reporting. Core Eligibility Characteristics Target businesses should generally meet the following criteria: 1. Women-led or women-majority-owned The business should be led by women or majority-owned by women. 2. Established business model Applicants should have a functioning and established business model rather than an idea-stage enterprise. 3. Formal or registered operation The initiative will prioritize registered or formally operating businesses. 4. Climate adaptation relevance The SME should demonstrate either: Existing climate adaptation practices, or Meaningful exposure to climate risks. 5. Existing operational evidence Applicants should have some existing information that can potentially be organized into useful evidence. This may include: Production data Market data Operational records Adoption data Extension information Business performance data Customer information Climate-related observations 6. Interest in climate finance or investment The SME should demonstrate an interest in using its adaptation evidence for purposes such as: Climate finance Investor engagement Business growth Adaptation learning Climate-responsive business development 7. Agribusiness value-chain participation The initiative welcomes representation across different functions of agricultural and food-system value chains. These may include: Production Processing Aggregation Input distribution Logistics Advisory services Market access What Kind of Support Will Selected SMEs Receive? The proposed facility will combine several forms of support rather than relying on financial assistance alone. 1. Small Grants Selected SMEs will receive small grants as part of the facility. These grants are intended to complement technical assistance and evidence-development activities. The broader objective is not simply to provide funding, but to help SMEs strengthen their ability to demonstrate and communicate the climate adaptation value of their businesses. 2. Technical Assistance Participating SMEs will receive technical assistance focused on areas such as: Climate adaptation evidence Data organization Impact measurement Climate-risk assessment Evidence validation Evidence packaging Business narratives Climate finance readiness Investor engagement 3. Climate Adaptation Masterclasses CGIAR’s technical expertise will support learning opportunities and masterclasses that can strengthen participating businesses understanding of climate adaptation and evidence. Potential areas include: Understanding climate risks Tracking adaptation Measuring resilience Organizing business evidence Communicating adaptation results Linking evidence to investment Understanding climate finance requirements 4. Evidence Packaging A central feature of the facility is helping SMEs transform scattered business information into structured evidence. Instead of leaving climate adaptation information inside operational records, participating businesses will be supported to develop clearer evidence products. These could help communicate: The climate challenge The business response The adaptation intervention The evidence available Business outcomes Resilience outcomes Potential for scale Finance needs 5. Climate Finance Readiness Support Participating SMEs will also be supported to understand how adaptation evidence can strengthen their ability to engage with potential climate finance and investment opportunities. The objective is to connect the technical climate evidence with commercially relevant business information. This can help businesses better explain: Climate risk → Adaptation action → Evidence → Business value → Investment opportunity The Proposed Intervention Model The facility follows a structured pathway designed to move from identification to evidence generation and ultimately toward finance, policy, and learning applications. The proposed pathway is: Identify → Select → Onboard → Support → Document → Validate → Package → Synthesize → Mobilize → Learn Component 1: VALUE4HER-Based Targeting, Expression of Interest, and SME Selection The initiative will begin by identifying potential women-led agribusiness SMEs through VALUE4HER and related AGRA partner pipelines. An Expression of Interest (EOI) process will be used to identify businesses that demonstrate: An established business model Climate adaptation relevance Existing evidence potential Some data capacity Interest in technical assistance Interest in climate finance readiness Interest in investor engagement The selection process will aim to balance readiness and inclusion . This means that businesses will not necessarily need to have sophisticated monitoring and evaluation systems already in place. Promising women-led SMEs should not be excluded simply because their evidence systems are still developing. Instead, the facility is designed to help businesses strengthen and organize the evidence they already possess. How the Selection Process Is Expected to Work The selection approach is intended to identify SMEs with both strong potential and a genuine need for support. The process may consider the following dimensions: Business readiness Established operations Business model strength Years of operation Registration status Growth potential Climate relevance Exposure to climate risks Existing adaptation activities Role in climate-resilient value chains Potential contribution to resilience Evidence potential Availability of existing data Operational records Production information Market data Adoption information Monitoring systems Finance readiness Interest in investment Interest in climate finance Existing financing needs Ability to articulate business opportunities Potential for future scale Inclusion and representation Selection will also seek appropriate representation across different agribusiness value-chain functions and different business contexts. Evidence Synthesis and Knowledge Generation The initiative will not only benefit individual SMEs. A broader objective is to generate a synthesized evidence base on women-led climate adaptation within African agribusiness. The evidence generated through participating businesses can contribute to a better understanding of: How women-led SMEs are responding to climate risks Which adaptation practices are being implemented What business benefits are associated with adaptation What evidence SMEs already possess Where evidence gaps remain What types of technical support businesses need What barriers limit climate finance access How adaptation evidence can support investment How women’s adaptation contributions can be better recognized This synthesis can support future learning, reporting, policy engagement, investment discussions, and potential scaling. Strategic Alignment The facility aligns strongly with the mandate and priorities of both VALUE4HER/AGRA and CGIAR. Alignment with VALUE4HER The initiative builds on VALUE4HER s existing focus on strengthening women-led agribusinesses through: Finance access Market access Technology Mentorship Networking Capacity building The proposed facility adds a climate adaptation evidence and finance-readiness dimension to that existing value proposition. This can enable women-led businesses to demonstrate not only that they are commercially active, but also that they contribute to resilience and climate adaptation. Alignment with AGRA The initiative is aligned with AGRA priorities around: Women s economic empowerment Climate adaptation SME development Inclusive food systems Resilient agricultural value chains It creates a practical link between women s entrepreneurship and climate action. Alignment with CGIAR The initiative draws directly on CGIAR capabilities in: Climate adaptation tracking Impact measurement Risk intelligence Climate finance readiness Evidence synthesis Gender-responsive adaptation tools The partnership therefore provides a bridge between technical climate research and the operational realities of women-led agribusiness SMEs. Proposed Implementation Period The proposed implementation period is: August–December 2026 The initiative is expected to progress through several stages during this period. August 2026 Initial activities are expected to focus on: SME identification Targeting Expression of Interest Selection Following selection The selected SMEs will move through: Onboarding Small-grant support Technical assistance Climate adaptation evidence organization Evidence packaging Climate finance readiness support Later stages The initiative will then focus on: Evidence synthesis Learning Climate finance mobilization support Policy engagement Adaptation reporting Dissemination of lessons Is There an Application Deadline? The information provided for this opportunity specifies an implementation period of August–December 2026 , but does not state a specific application or Expression of Interest deadline . Applicants and interested women-led agribusiness SMEs should therefore verify the official EOI announcement or VALUE4HER/AGRA communication for the exact submission deadline before applying. Geographic and Country Eligibility The initiative focuses on Africa , drawing primarily on the VALUE4HER network, which spans 46 African countries . The opportunity is therefore intended for eligible women-led agribusiness SMEs operating within Africa rather than applicants from countries outside the African continent. Click HERE to read more. Sector Eligibility Eligible businesses should be connected to agribusiness and agricultural or food-system value chains. Relevant areas include: Agricultural production Processing Aggregation Input distribution Logistics Agricultural advisory services Market access Other relevant agribusiness activities What Makes a Strong Candidate? A particularly strong candidate would be a woman-led agribusiness that can demonstrate both commercial activity and climate relevance . For example, a strong candidate could have: An established business A clear business model A woman founder, owner, or majority ownership structure Exposure to climate risks Existing adaptation practices Existing business or operational records A clear need for better evidence Interest in climate finance Interest in investment Potential for growth and scale Importantly, businesses do not necessarily need to have highly sophisticated climate monitoring systems. The initiative specifically recognizes that evidence systems may still be emerging and seeks to strengthen businesses that have promising practices and useful information that can be organized and developed. APPLY HERE Broader Significance for Women and Climate Action Women are central to agricultural and food systems across Africa, yet their contributions to climate adaptation are not always adequately represented in formal evidence and financing systems. Women-led SMEs can occupy critical positions between producers, markets, consumers, suppliers, financial institutions, and other actors. Supporting these enterprises can therefore have implications beyond individual businesses. Strengthening their evidence can help demonstrate how women entrepreneurs contribute to: Climate-resilient food systems Agricultural adaptation Business resilience Local economic development Innovation Market resilience Inclusive investment Gender-responsive climate action The initiative consequently addresses both a business evidence gap and a gender-responsive climate adaptation gap . Key Takeaway The VALUE4HER Climate Adaptation Evidence and Finance Readiness Facility is designed to help women-led agribusiness SMEs move from unrecognized climate adaptation activity to credible, finance-relevant evidence . The initiative combines: VALUE4HER s continental SME network + AGRA s climate expertise + CGIAR s adaptation research and technical capabilities to create a practical pathway through which women-led businesses can document what they are already doing, demonstrate the value of their adaptation activities, strengthen their finance readiness, and contribute to a broader understanding of women s role in climate resilience. Conclusion The VALUE4HER Climate Adaptation Evidence and Finance Readiness Facility for Women-Led Agribusiness SMEs represents an opportunity to close an important gap between climate action, evidence, and finance. Across Africa, women-led agribusinesses are already responding to climate risks through innovation, business adaptation, market diversification, improved production systems, processing, logistics, advisory services, input distribution, and other activities across food and agricultural value chains. Yet many of these contributions remain invisible because businesses may lack the systems, technical capacity, or resources required to transform operational information into credible climate adaptation evidence. title: Catalyst Now Learning Initiatives Fellow 2026: Remote Global Fellowship with $750 Monthly Stipend
summary: Catalyst Now is inviting applications for its Learning Initiatives Fellow opportunity, a six-month remote position designed for individuals interested in learning coordination, programme management, community engagement, communications, social innovation and global network development. The opportunity provides the chance to work with a dynamic international team supporting learning initiatives that bring together social innovators, entrepreneurs, facilitators and organisations from around the world. The successful candidate will contribute to the planning and delivery of the Learning Series, Fundraising Masterclasses and Academic Hubs , while helping Catalyst Now strengthen participation, documentation, monitoring and knowledge management across its global learning activities. The position is remote and can be undertaken from most regions provided applicants can maintain approximately five hours of working-time overlap with Central European Summer Time (CEST). The fellowship is scheduled to begin in early September 2026 . Applications must be submitted by August 31, 2026 , although Catalyst Now will review applications on a rolling basis and may fill the position before the stated deadline. The organisation brings together a broad network that includes grassroots initiatives, social entrepreneurs, philanthropic organisations and other actors involved in social innovation. Catalyst Now s mission is to create spaces where social innovators can: Connect with people and organisations working on similar challenges. Collaborate across sectors, countries and disciplines. Share knowledge, experience and practical solutions. Contribute to transformational and systemic change. Strengthen the visibility and impact of social innovation initiatives. The movement has grown from its beginnings as a WhatsApp group of social entrepreneurs into an international network representing thousands of social innovators and organisations across more than 150 countries. Its broader vision recognises that the world already has many potential solutions to challenges such as climate change, inequality, health, livelihoods and the Sustainable Development Goals. However, many solutions remain disconnected from the resources, policies, networks and institutions necessary to achieve systemic impact. Catalyst Now therefore seeks to help create greater alignment among social innovators and connect fragmented efforts with broader systems of change. About the Learning Initiatives Fellow Opportunity The Learning Initiatives Fellow will support the coordination and implementation of Catalyst Now s systems-learning activities. The role is particularly focused on the organisation s Learning Series and Fundraising Masterclasses , while also providing coordination support to the Academic Hubs. This is a highly coordination-oriented opportunity. The Fellow will help ensure that learning sessions are properly planned, facilitators have the resources they need, participants receive timely information and data relating to attendance, feedback and engagement is accurately recorded. The successful candidate will work across several teams, including the Community Building and Learning team and Communications team. The role will also involve regular interaction with facilitators, speakers, participants and other contributors. Because the position involves managing several activities simultaneously, strong organisation, communication, attention to detail and follow-through are particularly important. Initiative Planning and Coordination The Fellow will play an important role in coordinating learning activities from the initial planning stage through to post-session follow-up. Responsibilities include: Coordinating the end-to-end delivery of Learning Series sessions. Supporting the delivery of Fundraising Masterclasses. Providing coordination assistance to the Academic Hubs. Developing and maintaining session timelines. Creating and updating checklists and activity plans. Coordinating session dates through shared team calendars. Identifying possible scheduling conflicts before they affect delivery. Monitoring upcoming initiatives and deadlines. Maintaining an overview of team responsibilities. Ensuring tasks are completed before, during and after each session. Following up on outstanding activities and deliverables. This aspect of the position requires someone who can keep track of multiple moving parts and ensure that important details are not overlooked. 2. Facilitator and Contributor Coordination The Fellow will also support the organisation s engagement with facilitators, speakers and other contributors. This may involve: Supporting the identification of suitable facilitators and speakers. Assisting with facilitator onboarding. Coordinating invitations. Organising briefing calls. Sending preparatory information. Sharing learning objectives and session formats. Communicating timelines and expectations. Following up on presentations and other materials. Collecting facilitator biographies. Collecting headshots and relevant resources. Providing logistical assistance before and during sessions. Strong interpersonal communication will therefore be useful because the Fellow will need to maintain professional and timely communication with people from different backgrounds and locations. 3. Participant Communication and Engagement Participant experience is another important component of the role. The Fellow will help ensure that participants have the information necessary to successfully attend and participate in learning activities. Responsibilities include: Maintaining participant mailing lists. Updating mailing lists for Learning Series activities. Managing lists for Fundraising Masterclasses. Preparing invitations. Sending session reminders. Providing joining instructions. Sending follow-up communications. Using mail merge and similar tools to personalise communications at scale. Responding to participant questions. Helping participants resolve basic logistical issues. Supporting initiatives aimed at improving attendance. Supporting efforts to increase participant engagement. Contributing to an improved overall participant experience. This responsibility makes the role particularly relevant to candidates with backgrounds in communications, community management, programme coordination, customer or participant engagement, education and events. 4. Virtual Session Delivery Because many Catalyst Now learning activities take place online, the Fellow will support the practical delivery of virtual sessions. Tasks may include: Setting up virtual meeting sessions. Coordinating meeting links and invitations. Checking technical requirements. Supporting facilitators and speakers during live sessions. Assisting participants with logistical issues. Monitoring attendance. Addressing technical or coordination challenges when they arise. Working with colleagues to ensure everyone understands their role. Ensuring session recordings are properly captured. Ensuring supporting materials are appropriately stored. Experience with virtual event platforms can therefore be an advantage. 5. Communications Coordination The Fellow will work with the Communications team to support visibility and promotion of learning initiatives. This includes: Submitting communication requests for social media promotion. Coordinating promotional timelines. Providing session information to communications colleagues. Sharing facilitator information and supporting materials. Ensuring promotional requirements are communicated clearly. Requesting publication of session recordings on YouTube or other relevant platforms. Reviewing communication materials for accuracy. Helping ensure information remains consistent across different communication channels. Candidates with communications experience may find this aspect of the role particularly relevant. 6. Monitoring, Feedback and Reporting The Learning Initiatives Fellow will contribute to monitoring the reach and quality of Catalyst Now s learning initiatives. Responsibilities include: Collecting attendance data. Collecting participant feedback. Monitoring participant satisfaction. Calculating satisfaction ratings according to the agreed methodology. Preparing brief reports. Documenting participation levels. Capturing key participant insights. Identifying areas for improvement. Tracking progress against Systems Initiatives Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Identifying recurring patterns in participant feedback. Supporting improvements to future sessions. Contributing to periodic reporting on programme reach, quality and outcomes. This means the position is not limited to event administration. The Fellow will also help the organisation understand what is working, what participants value and where future learning activities can be improved. 7. Documentation and Knowledge Management Accurate documentation is another major component of the role. The Fellow will help maintain: Participant records. Session reports. Presentations. Session recordings. Communication materials. Feedback information. Reporting documents. Templates. Guides. Checklists. Process documentation. The successful candidate will also be expected to: Store materials in the appropriate shared drives. Keep organisational documents properly organised. Update templates and process documents when necessary. Document lessons emerging from learning initiatives. Record improvements that can support future programme delivery. Maintain appropriate confidentiality and data protection practices. Good attention to detail and familiarity with digital file-management systems will therefore be important. 8. Team Collaboration The Fellow will work collaboratively with colleagues across Catalyst Now. The role involves collaboration with: Systems Learning colleagues. Community Building colleagues. Learning team members. Communications staff. Facilitators. Speakers. Other internal contributors. The Fellow may also participate in: Planning meetings. Team check-ins. Programme coordination discussions. Post-session reflections. Review meetings. Candidates should be comfortable working independently while also knowing when to communicate risks, delays or requests for support. Qualifications and Experience Required Catalyst Now is seeking applicants with a background or equivalent experience relevant to programme coordination, project management, communications, education, international development or social innovation. Applicants should ideally have: A bachelor s degree or equivalent professional experience. Experience in programme coordination or project management. Experience coordinating learning sessions, events, webinars or community programmes. Experience communicating with participants and facilitators. Experience working with internal and external stakeholders. Strong organisational skills. The ability to manage multiple deadlines. Experience collecting and organising programme or participant data. What Would Success Look Like? Catalyst Now has identified several indicators that can demonstrate successful performance in the role.
